The agreement was part of the **1951 NATO founding treaty** and was later incorporated into the **1952 U.S.-Denmark Defense Agreement**, which formalized U.S. military access to Greenland under the **North Atlantic Treaty**. The **1951 framework** (inference) is believed to have granted the U.S. rights to establish military facilities in Greenland in exchange for defense support, but the precise wording was likely a **bilateral exchange** (not widely archived in public sources). **Key uncertainties:** 1. The **1952 Defense Agreement** (the more accessible document) expanded upon it but may not fully reflect the original 1951 terms. 3. **No direct text** of the 1951 agreement exists in the verified findings or public web archives (observation). **Concrete Test:** To resolve this, **query the public archives for:** 1. **The full text of the 1952 U.S.-Denmark Defense Agreement** (which may reference the 1951 understanding). 2. **Declassified U.S. State Department or Danish Foreign Ministry records** from 1951 (if available in the public domain). 3. **NATO’s founding documents** (1949) for any indirect references to Greenland’s status in the early treaty. **Expected outcome:** - If the **1952 agreement** explicitly cites the 1951 terms, that would clarify the original intent. - If **no direct text** is found, the **1952 agreement** would serve as the closest available proxy (inference). - **Uncertainty remains** if the 1951 agreement was purely oral or informal (no public record).
